Read the following technical documentation. Summarize the main implementation constraints and the benchmark methodology.

# DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash MXFP4: local RTX 5090 envelope

This branch runs DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (GGUF arch `deepseek41`) with its routed experts kept in the
released MXFP4 precision, on the same single-GPU, 16 GiB envelope as the Kimi K3 work. This page
records the code, the assets, how correctness was checked, and the measured operating points.

## Code

The runtime is a port of the upstream DeepSeek-V4.1 support from vcruz305/llama.cpp
`runtime/deepseek41` @ 5210c7c. This fork's own `DEEPSEEK4` port is a different design and is left
unchanged. Differences from upstream: of the fused hyper-connection kernels, the Sinkhorn combination and
the expansion (`dsv4_hc_comb`, `dsv4_hc_post`) are ported, while the pre collapse uses this fork's
`hc_weighted_sum` (the same sum as `dsv4_hc_pre`), and `LLAMA_DSV41_HC_FUSED=0` builds the plain-op graph
instead (see [Fused hyper-connection ops](#fused-hyper-connection-ops)); `wo_a` is reshaped in the graph
instead of at load, there is no MTP/DSpark
graph and no rollback planes in the cache (`n_rs_seq` must be 0), and the two-level candidate mask is
not implemented (same as upstream).

## Assets

- GGUF: `vcruz305/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-GGUF`, the `Q8_0` rung, 10 shards, 507.95 GB. Routed experts are
  stored as MXFP4 and are bit-identical to the official FP4 weights (sampled rows from layers 0 and 39,
  gate/up/down, experts 0 and 383, dequantize to the same values). Dense tensors are Q8_0 (from FP8) and
  BF16; the two engram tables are Q8_0 (from FP8). All experts are in shards 1-7, the engram tables in
  shards 8 and 9, everything else in shard 10.

## Correctness

Both checks compare against a build of the upstream branch on the same host.

1. Tiny random `deepseek41` model (6 layers, compressed layers at ratios 2 and 1, engram on layer 1),
   `llama-eval-callback`, named tensors: on CPU all 303 matched tensors agree within 1e-3 relative
   sum error; routed and shared expert outputs are identical, engram output 1.7e-7, attention output
   at most 8.6e-5, and the indexer selects the same positions. On CUDA the differences (1e-3 to
   4.5e-3) are the same size as the upstream build's own CPU-vs-CUDA differences.
2. Real model, greedy decoding with `ignore_eos`, 16 tokens on two prompts, top-5 logprobs recorded:
   the port and upstream produce identical tokens on CPU-only and on CUDA. Chosen-token logprob gaps
   (port vs upstream, CPU: mean 0.07, max 0.26) are within the upstream build's own CPU-vs-CUDA spread
   (mean 0.10, max 0.58); this model amplifies small numeric differences through expert selection, so
   compare token ids rather than logprobs.
3. Real-model prefill pack-source OFF/ON checks used a 52-token prompt and a 436-token, seven-pass
   prompt. Every ON arm completed all reads through io_uring with zero fallback; first-token values
   and top-10 logits were bit-identical between OFF and ON.

`llama-eval-callback` crashes on the real model in both builds; do not use it there.

## Build

Same flags as the K3 branch (CUDA 13.0, RTX 5090):

```sh
cmake -S . -B build-dsv41 \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON \
  -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS=-ffp-contract=off -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS=-ffp-contract=off \
  -DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER=/usr/local/cuda-13.0/bin/nvcc \
  -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_NATIVE=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120a \
  -DGGML_CUDA_MOE_STREAM_BATCH=ON -DGGML_CUDA_KIMI_VRAM_TIER=ON \
  -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF
cmake --build build-dsv41 --parallel 8 --target llama-server llama-cli
```

## Host and envelope

Measurements ran on a local test server standing in for the target machine:

| | Test server | Target envelope |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | Core Ultra 5 230F, 10 cores, AVX2 + AVX-VNNI | 16 threads (Core Ultra 7 255H) |
| Memory | 30 GB, limited to 16 GiB, no swap | 16 GiB |
| GPU | RTX 5090 32 GB, PCIe Gen5 x16, host-to-device copies paced at 7 GB/s by `libh2dgov` (shared link model) | RTX 5090 behind PCIe Gen4 x4 |
| NVMe | Gen5 x4 (ZHITAI TiPro9000 4TB); 11.5 GiB/s sustained for the sink's 6.27 MB slices in its normal state, 4-9 GiB/s in a degraded state after large writes ([SSD state](#ssd-state)) | Gen5 x4 |

The server has fewer CPU cores than the target, so CPU-bound configurations are conservative here.
`.Agent/run-tools/dsv41/run-envelope.sh` applies the envelope
(`systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p AllowedCPUs=0-9`,
`LD_PRELOAD=libh2dgov.so H2D_GOV_GBPS=7 H2D_GOV_MODE=wait`, `taskset -c 0-9`) and runs
`bench_v41.py` (greedy `/completion`, `ignore_eos`, prompt excluded from the decode rate).

The elastic-arena phase-2 measurements used a changed host setup: CPU governor `performance` and a
600 W GPU power limit. An attempted 3,135 MHz SM lock did not hold: all 9,467 samples were
2,947/2,955 MHz, including every loaded sample. THP was temporarily `always`, but the expert cache is
explicitly `MADV_NOHUGEPAGE` and had zero `AnonHugePages`. The ineffective clock lock and THP setting
were reverted after the round. The elastic tok/s values therefore are not directly comparable with
speed measurements made before `73b6179f9`; the deterministic cache and byte counters are the primary
evidence.

The later dynamic-row round kept the CPU governor at `performance`, restored the GPU power limit to
575 W, and used the effective GPU lock: loaded `clocks.sm` min/median/max was
2,940/2,947/2,955 MHz. NVMe runtime PM stayed `auto` and system THP stayed `madvise`. None of these
host settings changed during the round.

The prefill O_DIRECT round used the same 7 GB/s shared H2D model. A 30-second shaped fio check read
12.26 GB/s, while valid ON arms read the expert pack at about 6.264 GB/s. The prefill path is therefore
bounded by the Gen4 x4 / 7 GB/s H2D envelope, not by this NVMe; a faster replacement drive alone does
not improve it.

### Host-to-device link model

`libh2dgov` books every host-to-device copy on a virtual 7 GB/s link and holds the copy's CUDA stream
until the virtual completion (a stream wait released by a helper thread), so the issuing thread never
blocks. Since 2026-09-15 18:00 the link is shared (`H2D_GOV_LINK=shared`, the default): the copies of
one stream complete in order, and the rate is split equally among the streams that have a copy in
flight. Every run before that used one FIFO clock across all streams (`H2D_GOV_LINK=fifo`), under which
a small copy waited for every copy booked before it on any stream.

The real card does not queue copies across streams. Without the governor
(`.Agent/run-tools/q3ks/h2d/h2d_overlap_probe.c`, Gen5 x16), a small copy on a second stream, issued
by another thread while a large copy was in flight:

| Large copy | Small copy (16 KiB) | Small copy latency | Large copy still in flight |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 GiB pinned, 40 ms | pinned, issued after 10 ms | 13-14 µs (6.5 µs alone) | 30 ms |
| 2 GiB pageable, 134 ms | pinned, issued after 20 ms | 9-25 µs | 114 ms |
| 2 GiB pageable, 134 ms | pageable, issued after 20 ms | 10-16 µs | 114 ms |
| Expert uploads: 20 experts x 3 pageable 6,266,880-byte roles, 0.24 ms per role | pinned or pageable, repeatedly | median 15 µs, at most 29 µs (5.3 µs alone) | - |

With the same upload burst under the governor, the FIFO clock held each small copy for 2.49 ms (the rest
of the expert's three roles); the shared link for 9 µs at the median and at most 36 µs, while the
uploads still ran at 6.9 GB/s. Two 512 MiB copies issued 20 ms apart on two streams finish after 133.3
and 153.4 ms, 7.00 GB/s together. The FIFO library also had a release race: its single completion
counter could step back when copies booked by two threads returned in the other order (a pageable copy
blocks, a pinned one returns at once), leaving a stream to wait for a later copy's completion; the probe
stalled on it. The shared link keeps one counter per stream.

On the real forms the link model hardly matters. Same binary and drive state, median of three requests
per run, all CPU sink forms with engram row prefetch (`seq-govshared.sh` and `seq-govextra.sh`,
2026-09-15 18:19-19:17):

| Form | FIFO clock | Shared link |
|---|---|---|
| `vram21` | 5.81, 5.85 tok/s | 5.88, 5.93 tok/s |
| `vram21_gpu_chain` | 5.98, 6.00 tok/s | 6.01, 6.09 tok/s |
| `vram21_mc15_hl8` (order fifo, shared, fifo, shared) | 5.41, 5.47 tok/s | 5.42, 5.45 tok/s |

With the sink profile (`vram21` + prefetch, one measured request) a decode token took 174.3 ms on the
shared link and 174.1 ms on the FIFO clock, with 16.1 and 16.2 ms of VRAM tier wait and 27.4 and
27.8 ms of expert uploads on the tier worker; without the governor it took 167.3 ms, 6.8 ms and
18.1 ms. The tier worker runs one job at a time and the layer finish drains the uploads, so a compute
copy could only wait for the tail of one expert upload, and the governor's statistics show less than
0.5 ms with two streams in flight over each run's 25,000-65,000 copies (0.15 s in the synthetic burst
above). What the governor adds to the tier is the uploads' own time at 7 GB/s, which the target's link
pays as well.

## CPU sink

The Kimi K3 CPU sink (`GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK=1`) streams routed experts from the expert pack with
io_uring `O_DIRECT` reads and computes them on CPU during single-token decode. For this model:

- Kernels follow the expert tensor type: MXFP4 weights use `vec_dot_mxfp4_q8_0` with a Q8_0-quantized
  input, exactly as CPU `MUL_MAT_ID` does, so results are bitwise identical to the normal CPU-experts
  path. Up and gate must share a type; down may differ.
- A second activation, SwiGLU with the V4.1 clamp (`silu(min(g, L)) * clamp(u, -L, L)`, per-layer `L`),
  sits next to K3's SiTU (`kimi_cpu_sink_run_activation`; `kimi_cpu_sink_run` is the SiTU wrapper).
- The pack resolver takes the slice size and the routed expert count from the tensor
  (`ggml_cuda_moe_expert_pack_resolve_direct_shape`); `CACHE_MAX_PER_LAYER` is capped at `n_expert`.
- `--defer-experts` keeps V4.1 routed experts in mmap-backed CPU buffers, so they never reach VRAM.
- Cache compute remains refused for V4.1. The default profile keeps the historical split: below the
  `GGML_OP_OFFLOAD_MIN_BATCH` gate (default 32), prefill runs experts through CPU `MUL_MAT_ID` on the
  deferred mmap GGUF; at or above the gate the scheduler uses GPU op offload and sources expert
  copies from the pack. The non-default `hybrid_prefill_u2048` profile instead enables
  `GGML_KIMI_CPU_PREFILL`: an ubatch-wide expert union runs on CPU while retained decode-tier hits run
  concurrently on GPU. The later `hybrid_prefill_adaptive_u2048` profile adds
  exact physical graph shapes, demand-driven arena reclaim and read-only RAM-cache
  sources. See `.Agent/profiles/20260921-deepseek-v41-prefill-optimization.md`.
- `GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_CACHE_RECLAIMABLE_FILE=1` (default 0) lets the RAM cache guard count the scope's
  `inactive_file` pages as headroom.
- `GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_DYNAMIC_ROWS=1` lets all CPU compute participants claim aligned row blocks from
  a shared cursor. `GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_DYNAMIC_CHUNK_ROWS` is a multiple of 16 (default 64); the
  runtime feature defaults off, and only `vram21_gpu_chain` opts in. It is mutually exclusive with
  static `ROW_WEIGHTS`; the `(ith,nth)` parallel callback keeps its existing ownership ABI.

Checks: `test-kimi-cpu-sink` passes its new activation cases (bitwise, threads 2/16, ring 1/8,
READY_FIRST 0/1); the 20 failing cases fail identically on the tree without these changes (they need
12-16 allowed CPUs, locked memory for io_uring, or a 120 GB sparse mapping). On the real model the
sink's logits are bitwise equal to the `-ot 'ffn_(up|gate|down)_exps=CPU'` build over 32 greedy tokens,
with and without an 8 GiB RAM cache, and every measured arm below produces the same greedy tokens as
the naive offload.

## Prefill expert-pack source

`GGML_SCHED_MOE_COPY_EXPERT_PACK_SOURCE=1` replaces the GGUF-mmap source of GPU op-offload expert
copies with the existing expert pack. The scheduler coalesces adjacent selected experts into ranges,
then the CUDA adapter reads them through io_uring and `O_DIRECT` into a 16-slot pinned staging ring.
The runtime master switch remains off so unrelated models and profiles retain their previous path;
`vram21_gpu_chain` explicitly enables it together with:

- `GGML_SCHED_MOE_COPY_EXPERT_PACK_SOURCE_PROMPT_ONLY=1`, so decode behavior remains on its existing
  source path;
- `GGML_SCHED_MOE_COPY_EXPERT_PACK_SOURCE_BATCH=1`, for coalesced range reads; and
- `GGML_SCHED_MOE_COPY_EXPERT_PACK_SOURCE_CACHE_BYPASS=1`, which leaves the decode RAM cache intact
  but skips prompt lookup and admission. A warm-cache isolation run hit only 10.20% of prompt expert
  bytes and did not reduce H2D bytes, so prompt cache participation only added work.

Any unavailable or failed direct range read falls back to the original mmap copy. The formal ON arms
did not take that fallback: 9,792 reads for the short prompt and 74,223 reads / 465,146,634,240 bytes
for each long prompt all completed directly. OFF and ON first-token values and top-10 logits were
bit-identical.

The formal round used three valid paired repetitions for a 52-token short prompt and three for a
436-token, seven-pass long prompt. Long-prompt geometric wall time fell from 216.108 to 74.262 seconds
(2.910x); ON effective read rate was about 6.264 GB/s. The 7 GB/s H2D governor, rather than the
12.26 GB/s shaped fio result, is the binding ceiling. Decode's paired geometric point estimate was
-1.97%, but the OFF interval (6.4921-6.5772 tok/s) overlaps the ON interval
(6.3031-6.6003 tok/s); this round does not establish a separated decode regression and must not be
reported as "no impact."

The capacity result is the main deployment effect. Peak `file-shmem` fell from
15.2277-15.2287 GiB to 0.0760-0.0791 GiB (-99.49%). `memory.peak` fell from exactly
17,179,869,184 bytes in every OFF arm to 11,825,610,752-11,830,030,336 bytes in ON arms. The latter
reduction is 5.35 GB, or 4.99 GiB; calling it 5.35 GiB would mix decimal and binary units. This removes
the prefill page-cache constraint that blocked a larger retained RAM cache.

The stage-3 raw CTest run registered 203 tests and reported 123 failed or not run, compared with the
known 121-name branch baseline. The only added names were `test-alloc` and `test-eval-callback`: the
known `test-mtmd-c-api` header failure had interrupted the aggregate build before those two binaries
were made. Building them separately and running their fixtures passed 3/3, so code-attributed new
failures were zero. The landing-only pack-plan test was added after that recorded full-suite run and
passes with the four related focused tests.

This change removes page-cache amplification; it is necessary but not sufficient for a production
100k prompt. With u-batch 64, the current estimate remains about 4.6 hours. Raising u-batch to 2048
brings the estimate to about 37.7 minutes, so deployment must combine direct expert reads with the
larger u-batch rather than claiming that O_DIRECT alone solves 100k prefill.

## VRAM expert tier

The CPU sink forms use 9.3 GB of the 32 GB card, which leaves room for about 1,100 routed experts
(18.8 MB each). The Kimi VRAM tier now serves them for this model: hot experts live in a VRAM arena
and are computed on the GPU, misses keep going through the RAM cache and the pack.

- Explicit-format tier ABI (`kimi_vram_format_get_api`): the sink passes the expert tensor geometry
  (types, expert count, layer list) and the activation; the Kimi-K3 Q3_K/SiTU path keeps the original
  ABI unchanged. Slot geometry and role sizes come from the tensors.
- Parity kernel (`libkimi-mxfp4-parity.so`, built with `--fmad=false --ftz=false`): MXFP4 x Q8_0 rows
  that reproduce the CPU `ggml_vec_dot_mxfp4_q8_0` AVX2 path bit for bit (eight int32 lanes of four
  products per block, FMA accumulators for even and odd blocks, the `hsum_float_8` order). Between the
  up/gate and down stages the host applies the sink's own clamped-SwiGLU expression and the linked CPU
  Q8_0 quantizer, so a GPU hit returns exactly what CPU `MUL_MAT_ID` would.
- Runtime parity gate: every MXFP4 engine checks itself when created (first decode token): 592
  deterministic rows at both column counts (5120 and 2304), realistic and edge E8M0 exponents, Q8_0
  inputs from the CPU quantizer, compared bit for bit with the linked CPU `vec_dot`. A mismatch (another
  CPU instruction set or compiler path) refuses the tier with the failing row named; there is no
  fallback and no override. The check takes about 1.4 ms and logs `mxfp4_selfcheck=pass`. With the
  GPU activation chain on, the check is skipped (the chain makes no bitwise claim) and the log says
  `mxfp4_selfcheck=skipped`.
- Policy: `count_decay2` over a global pool with admission above a minimum decayed selection count;
  a resident is never evicted for a colder candidate; exclusive residency drops the RAM copy of a VRAM
  resident. Uploads run asynchronously on the tier worker, borrow the bytes already read for the CPU
  path (no second host copy) and pass through `libh2dgov` at 7 GB/s.
  `GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_VRAM_KEEP_ACROSS_REQUESTS=1` keeps the arena through prefill.
- Deferred uploads (`GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_VRAM_DEFERRED_UPLOAD=1`, in the `vram21` and `vram21_gpu_chain`
  profiles): the layer no longer waits for its uploads; see [Deferred uploads](#deferred-uploads).
- Elastic global arena (`GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_VRAM_ELASTIC=1` in `vram21_gpu_chain`): release decode-only
  blocks before the next prefill reserve, let the CUDA backend allocator reclaim further blocks on OOM,
  then grow from free memory after the decode reserve; see
  [Elastic VRAM arena](#elastic-vram-arena-default-global-tier).
- Launch: preload `libkimi-no-mmap-prefetch.so:libkimi-mxfp4-parity.so:libkimi-vram-tier.so` (then
  `libh2dgov.so`), set `GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_VRAM_BYTES`, and the policy switches in
  `configs/deepseek-v41-flash-mxfp4/local-5090.json`.

Checks: component parity 148 checks, 0 unequal; the real sink with the tier against a CPU-only sink,
376,832 floats bitwise equal across exclusive/async/global-pool/RAM/keep modes, both shapes, epoch and
I/O-fault paths; both simulated CPU mismatches refused at the named check; the six Kimi-K3 tier tests
pass; `ctest` 87/107 with the same 20 environmental failures as before. On the real model every arm
with the tier produced the same greedy tokens as the naive offload.

Policy sweep at a 21 GB budget (one run each; disk bytes per token are deterministic, speeds for
information only; normal drive state):

| MIN_COUNT | Half-life | Disk GB/token | VRAM / RAM / SSD share of routed experts | Uploads per token (GB) | Decode tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 8 | 1.480 | 68.9 / 0.0 / 31.1 | 74.6 (1.40) | 2.99 |

## Correctness

Both checks compare against a build of the upstream branch on the same host.

1. Tiny random `deepseek41` model (6 layers, compressed layers at ratios 2 and 1, engram on layer 1),
   `llama-eval-callback`, named tensors: on CPU all 303 matched tensors agree within 1e-3 relative
   sum error; routed and shared expert outputs are identical, engram output 1.7e-7, attention output
   at most 8.6e-5, and the indexer selects the same positions. On CUDA the differences (1e-3 to
   4.5e-3) are the same size as the upstream build's own CPU-vs-CUDA differences.
2. Real model, greedy decoding with `ignore_eos`, 16 tokens on two prompts, top-5 logprobs recorded:
   the port and upstream produce identical tokens on CPU-only and on CUDA. Chosen-token logprob gaps
   (port vs upstream, CPU: mean 0.07, max 0.26) are within the upstream build's own CPU-vs-CUDA spread
   (mean 0.10, max 0.58); this model amplifies small numeric differences through expert selection, so
   compare token ids rather than logprobs.
3. Real-model prefill pack-source OFF/ON checks used a 52-token prompt and a 436-token, seven-pass
   prompt. Every ON arm completed all reads through io_uring with zero fallback; first-token values
   and top-10 logits were bit-identical between OFF and ON.

## Host and envelope

Measurements ran on a local test server standing in for the target machine:

| | Test server | Target envelope |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | Core Ultra 5 230F, 10 cores, AVX2 + AVX-VNNI | 16 threads (Core Ultra 7 255H) |
| Memory | 30 GB, limited to 16 GiB, no swap | 16 GiB |
| GPU | RTX 5090 32 GB, PCIe Gen5 x16, host-to-device copies paced at 7 GB/s by `libh2dgov` (shared link model) | RTX 5090 behind PCIe Gen4 x4 |
| NVMe | Gen5 x4 (ZHITAI TiPro9000 4TB); 11.5 GiB/s sustained for the sink's 6.27 MB slices in its normal state, 4-9 GiB/s in a degraded state after large writes ([SSD state](#ssd-state)) | Gen5 x4 |

The server has fewer CPU cores than the target, so CPU-bound configurations are conservative here.
`.Agent/run-tools/dsv41/run-envelope.sh` applies the envelope
(`systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p AllowedCPUs=0-9`,
`LD_PRELOAD=libh2dgov.so H2D_GOV_GBPS=7 H2D_GOV_MODE=wait`, `taskset -c 0-9`) and runs
`bench_v41.py` (greedy `/completion`, `ignore_eos`, prompt excluded from the decode rate).

The elastic-arena phase-2 measurements used a changed host setup: CPU governor `performance` and a
600 W GPU power limit. An attempted 3,135 MHz SM lock did not hold: all 9,467 samples were
2,947/2,955 MHz, including every loaded sample. THP was temporarily `always`, but the expert cache is
explicitly `MADV_NOHUGEPAGE` and had zero `AnonHugePages`. The ineffective clock lock and THP setting
were reverted after the round. The elastic tok/s values therefore are not directly comparable with
speed measurements made before `73b6179f9`; the deterministic cache and byte counters are the primary
evidence.

The later dynamic-row round kept the CPU governor at `performance`, restored the GPU power limit to
575 W, and used the effective GPU lock: loaded `clocks.sm` min/median/max was
2,940/2,947/2,955 MHz. NVMe runtime PM stayed `auto` and system THP stayed `madvise`. None of these
host settings changed during the round.

The prefill O_DIRECT round used the same 7 GB/s shared H2D model. A 30-second shaped fio check read
12.26 GB/s, while valid ON arms read the expert pack at about 6.264 GB/s. The prefill path is therefore
bounded by the Gen4 x4 / 7 GB/s H2D envelope, not by this NVMe; a faster replacement drive alone does
not improve it.

### Host-to-device link model

`libh2dgov` books every host-to-device copy on a virtual 7 GB/s link and holds the copy's CUDA stream
until the virtual completion (a stream wait released by a helper thread), so the issuing thread never
blocks. Since 2026-09-15 18:00 the link is shared (`H2D_GOV_LINK=shared`, the default): the copies of
one stream complete in order, and the rate is split equally among the streams that have a copy in
flight. Every run before that used one FIFO clock across all streams (`H2D_GOV_LINK=fifo`), under which
a small copy waited for every copy booked before it on any stream.

The real card does not queue copies across streams. Without the governor
(`.Agent/run-tools/q3ks/h2d/h2d_overlap_probe.c`, Gen5 x16), a small copy on a second stream, issued
by another thread while a large copy was in flight:

| Large copy | Small copy (16 KiB) | Small copy latency | Large copy still in flight |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 GiB pinned, 40 ms | pinned, issued after 10 ms | 13-14 µs (6.5 µs alone) | 30 ms |
| 2 GiB pageable, 134 ms | pinned, issued after 20 ms | 9-25 µs | 114 ms |
| 2 GiB pageable, 134 ms | pageable, issued after 20 ms | 10-16 µs | 114 ms |
| Expert uploads: 20 experts x 3 pageable 6,266,880-byte roles, 0.24 ms per role | pinned or pageable, repeatedly | median 15 µs, at most 29 µs (5.3 µs alone) | - |

With the same upload burst under the governor, the FIFO clock held each small copy for 2.49 ms (the rest
of the expert's three roles); the shared link for 9 µs at the median and at most 36 µs, while the
uploads still ran at 6.9 GB/s. Two 512 MiB copies issued 20 ms apart on two streams finish after 133.3
and 153.4 ms, 7.00 GB/s together. The FIFO library also had a release race: its single completion
counter could step back when copies booked by two threads returned in the other order (a pageable copy
blocks, a pinned one returns at once), leaving a stream to wait for a later copy's completion; the probe
stalled on it. The shared link keeps one counter per stream.

On the real forms the link model hardly matters. Same binary and drive state, median of three requests
per run, all CPU sink forms with engram row prefetch (`seq-govshared.sh` and `seq-govextra.sh`,
2026-09-15 18:19-19:17):

| Form | FIFO clock | Shared link |
|---|---|---|
| `vram21` | 5.81, 5.85 tok/s | 5.88, 5.93 tok/s |
| `vram21_gpu_chain` | 5.98, 6.00 tok/s | 6.01, 6.09 tok/s |
| `vram21_mc15_hl8` (order fifo, shared, fifo, shared) | 5.41, 5.47 tok/s | 5.42, 5.45 tok/s |

With the sink profile (`vram21` + prefetch, one measured request) a decode token took 174.3 ms on the
shared link and 174.1 ms on the FIFO clock, with 16.1 and 16.2 ms of VRAM tier wait and 27.4 and
27.8 ms of expert uploads on the tier worker; without the governor it took 167.3 ms, 6.8 ms and
18.1 ms. The tier worker runs one job at a time and the layer finish drains the uploads, so a compute
copy could only wait for the tail of one expert upload, and the governor's statistics show less than
0.5 ms with two streams in flight over each run's 25,000-65,000 copies (0.15 s in the synthetic burst
above). What the governor adds to the tier is the uploads' own time at 7 GB/s, which the target's link
pays as well.

## CPU sink

The Kimi K3 CPU sink (`GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK=1`) streams routed experts from the expert pack with
io_uring `O_DIRECT` reads and computes them on CPU during single-token decode. For this model:

- Kernels follow the expert tensor type: MXFP4 weights use `vec_dot_mxfp4_q8_0` with a Q8_0-quantized
  input, exactly as CPU `MUL_MAT_ID` does, so results are bitwise identical to the normal CPU-experts
  path. Up and gate must share a type; down may differ.
- A second activation, SwiGLU with the V4.1 clamp (`silu(min(g, L)) * clamp(u, -L, L)`, per-layer `L`),
  sits next to K3's SiTU (`kimi_cpu_sink_run_activation`; `kimi_cpu_sink_run` is the SiTU wrapper).
- The pack resolver takes the slice size and the routed expert count from the tensor
  (`ggml_cuda_moe_expert_pack_resolve_direct_shape`); `CACHE_MAX_PER_LAYER` is capped at `n_expert`.
- `--defer-experts` keeps V4.1 routed experts in mmap-backed CPU buffers, so they never reach VRAM.
- Cache compute remains refused for V4.1. The default profile keeps the historical split: below the
  `GGML_OP_OFFLOAD_MIN_BATCH` gate (default 32), prefill runs experts through CPU `MUL_MAT_ID` on the
  deferred mmap GGUF; at or above the gate the scheduler uses GPU op offload and sources expert
  copies from the pack. The non-default `hybrid_prefill_u2048` profile instead enables
  `GGML_KIMI_CPU_PREFILL`: an ubatch-wide expert union runs on CPU while retained decode-tier hits run
  concurrently on GPU. The later `hybrid_prefill_adaptive_u2048` profile adds
  exact physical graph shapes, demand-driven arena reclaim and read-only RAM-cache
  sources. See `.Agent/profiles/20260921-deepseek-v41-prefill-optimization.md`.
- `GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_CACHE_RECLAIMABLE_FILE=1` (default 0) lets the RAM cache guard count the scope's
  `inactive_file` pages as headroom.
- `GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_DYNAMIC_ROWS=1` lets all CPU compute participants claim aligned row blocks from
  a shared cursor. `GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_DYNAMIC_CHUNK_ROWS` is a multiple of 16 (default 64); the
  runtime feature defaults off, and only `vram21_gpu_chain` opts in. It is mutually exclusive with
  static `ROW_WEIGHTS`; the `(ith,nth)` parallel callback keeps its existing ownership ABI.

Checks: `test-kimi-cpu-sink` passes its new activation cases (bitwise, threads 2/16, ring 1/8,
READY_FIRST 0/1); the 20 failing cases fail identically on the tree without these changes (they need
12-16 allowed CPUs, locked memory for io_uring, or a 120 GB sparse mapping). On the real model the
sink's logits are bitwise equal to the `-ot 'ffn_(up|gate|down)_exps=CPU'` build over 32 greedy tokens,
with and without an 8 GiB RAM cache, and every measured arm below produces the same greedy tokens as
the naive offload.

## Prefill expert-pack source

`GGML_SCHED_MOE_COPY_EXPERT_PACK_SOURCE=1` replaces the GGUF-mmap source of GPU op-offload expert
copies with the existing expert pack. The scheduler coalesces adjacent selected experts into ranges,
then the CUDA adapter reads them through io_uring and `O_DIRECT` into a 16-slot pinned staging ring.
The runtime master switch remains off so unrelated models and profiles retain their previous path;
`vram21_gpu_chain` explicitly enables it together with:

- `GGML_SCHED_MOE_COPY_EXPERT_PACK_SOURCE_PROMPT_ONLY=1`, so decode behavior remains on its existing
  source path;
- `GGML_SCHED_MOE_COPY_EXPERT_PACK_SOURCE_BATCH=1`, for coalesced range reads; and
- `GGML_SCHED_MOE_COPY_EXPERT_PACK_SOURCE_CACHE_BYPASS=1`, which leaves the decode RAM cache intact
  but skips prompt lookup and admission. A warm-cache isolation run hit only 10.20% of prompt expert
  bytes and did not reduce H2D bytes, so prompt cache participation only added work.

Any unavailable or failed direct range read falls back to the original mmap copy. The formal ON arms
did not take that fallback: 9,792 reads for the short prompt and 74,223 reads / 465,146,634,240 bytes
for each long prompt all completed directly. OFF and ON first-token values and top-10 logits were
bit-identical.

The formal round used three valid paired repetitions for a 52-token short prompt and three for a
436-token, seven-pass long prompt. Long-prompt geometric wall time fell from 216.108 to 74.262 seconds
(2.910x); ON effective read rate was about 6.264 GB/s. The 7 GB/s H2D governor, rather than the
12.26 GB/s shaped fio result, is the binding ceiling. Decode's paired geometric point estimate was
-1.97%, but the OFF interval (6.4921-6.5772 tok/s) overlaps the ON interval
(6.3031-6.6003 tok/s); this round does not establish a separated decode regression and must not be
reported as "no impact."

The capacity result is the main deployment effect. Peak `file-shmem` fell from
15.2277-15.2287 GiB to 0.0760-0.0791 GiB (-99.49%). `memory.peak` fell from exactly
17,179,869,184 bytes in every OFF arm to 11,825,610,752-11,830,030,336 bytes in ON arms. The latter
reduction is 5.35 GB, or 4.99 GiB; calling it 5.35 GiB would mix decimal and binary units. This removes
the prefill page-cache constraint that blocked a larger retained RAM cache.

The stage-3 raw CTest run registered 203 tests and reported 123 failed or not run, compared with the
known 121-name branch baseline. The only added names were `test-alloc` and `test-eval-callback`: the
known `test-mtmd-c-api` header failure had interrupted the aggregate build before those two binaries
were made. Building them separately and running their fixtures passed 3/3, so code-attributed new
failures were zero. The landing-only pack-plan test was added after that recorded full-suite run and
passes with the four related focused tests.

This change removes page-cache amplification; it is necessary but not sufficient for a production
100k prompt. With u-batch 64, the current estimate remains about 4.6 hours. Raising u-batch to 2048
brings the estimate to about 37.7 minutes, so deployment must combine direct expert reads with the
larger u-batch rather than claiming that O_DIRECT alone solves 100k prefill.

## VRAM expert tier

The CPU sink forms use 9.3 GB of the 32 GB card, which leaves room for about 1,100 routed experts
(18.8 MB each). The Kimi VRAM tier now serves them for this model: hot experts live in a VRAM arena
and are computed on the GPU, misses keep going through the RAM cache and the pack.

- Explicit-format tier ABI (`kimi_vram_format_get_api`): the sink passes the expert tensor geometry
  (types, expert count, layer list) and the activation; the Kimi-K3 Q3_K/SiTU path keeps the original
  ABI unchanged. Slot geometry and role sizes come from the tensors.
- Parity kernel (`libkimi-mxfp4-parity.so`, built with `--fmad=false --ftz=false`): MXFP4 x Q8_0 rows
  that reproduce the CPU `ggml_vec_dot_mxfp4_q8_0` AVX2 path bit for bit (eight int32 lanes of four
  products per block, FMA accumulators for even and odd blocks, the `hsum_float_8` order). Between the
  up/gate and down stages the host applies the sink's own clamped-SwiGLU expression and the linked CPU
  Q8_0 quantizer, so a GPU hit returns exactly what CPU `MUL_MAT_ID` would.
- Runtime parity gate: every MXFP4 engine checks itself when created (first decode token): 592
  deterministic rows at both column counts (5120 and 2304), realistic and edge E8M0 exponents, Q8_0
  inputs from the CPU quantizer, compared bit for bit with the linked CPU `vec_dot`. A mismatch (another
  CPU instruction set or compiler path) refuses the tier with the failing row named; there is no
  fallback and no override. The check takes about 1.4 ms and logs `mxfp4_selfcheck=pass`. With the
  GPU activation chain on, the check is skipped (the chain makes no bitwise claim) and the log says
  `mxfp4_selfcheck=skipped`.
- Policy: `count_decay2` over a global pool with admission above a minimum decayed selection count;
  a resident is never evicted for a colder candidate; exclusive residency drops the RAM copy of a VRAM
  resident. Uploads run asynchronously on the tier worker, borrow the bytes already read for the CPU
  path (no second host copy) and pass through `libh2dgov` at 7 GB/s.
  `GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_VRAM_KEEP_ACROSS_REQUESTS=1` keeps the arena through prefill.
- Deferred uploads (`GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_VRAM_DEFERRED_UPLOAD=1`, in the `vram21` and `vram21_gpu_chain`
  profiles): the layer no longer waits for its uploads; see [Deferred uploads](#deferred-uploads).
- Elastic global arena (`GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_VRAM_ELASTIC=1` in `vram21_gpu_chain`): release decode-only
  blocks before the next prefill reserve, let the CUDA backend allocator reclaim further blocks on OOM,
  then grow from free memory after the decode reserve; see

## GPU activation chain (default, not bitwise)

`GGML_KIMI_CPU_SINK_VRAM_MXFP4_GPU_HIDDEN=1` (default 0) runs a layer's VRAM hits in one GPU submission.

quantization of the hidden rows and the down matvec all run on the device, and the unweighted down
